items.passage: Harvest makes fools of everyone. Dolores had said so for thirty seasons, and this year she said it chiefly about Esteban. Since the pickers she had trained without him had filled more baskets than any crew in Seville, the young man had taken to sulking beneath the olive tree at the end of the rows, as idle and decorative, she told the foreman, as a weathervane on a windless day. She complained of his boots, of his singing, of the way he still walked as if the whole slope belonged to him. She did not want him back on the crew; no, that was not quite it, either. Each evening, when the carts went down to the press, she counted the baskets aloud and paused at the blank space on the tally board where his name had once been chalked. On the last morning she rose before the others, walked the steep row he had always claimed, and left those vines unpicked until he came down from the tree.
items.question: Which choice best describes Dolores's attitude toward Esteban as it is conveyed in the passage?
options: She mocks his idleness while hoping the new crew will keep its record.
She shows him kindness while trying to ease her guilt over benching him.
She treats him as decorative while accepting the slope is no longer his.
She ridicules his sulking while holding a role for him in the work.
items.explanation: Dolores는 앞부분에서 Esteban의 게으름과 부츠, 노래를 비꼬며 불평하지만, 중간에 '그것도 꼭 맞는 말은 아니다'라며 스스로를 정정한다. 뒤에서는 장부의 빈칸에서 멈추고, 그가 늘 맡던 줄의 포도를 그가 올 때까지 따지 않고 남겨 두어 그의 자리를 비워 둔다. 따라서 말투 아래에서 그의 자리를 지켜 주는 태도를 말한 D가 정답이다. A는 말투만 읽었고, B는 죄책감이라는 근거 없는 이유를 대며, C는 지문 어휘(decorative, slope)를 빌렸지만 남겨 둔 포도와 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: Bergen rain had warped every shelf in the studio by the spring Thorvald came to replace them, and he let me know it was my fault for stacking wet pots too close together. He was a slow, grumbling man who measured each plank three times and talked to the wood more than to me. I said, often and loudly, that he worked like a glacier. Then my teacher looked at my first glazed bowl and remarked, within Thorvald's hearing, that I threw pots the way a carpenter joins wood: careful, square, and without any joy. I told myself I did not care what either of them thought. That is not entirely true, I suppose. Thorvald finished the shelves a week later. I noticed that he had sanded one corner of the lowest shelf round and smooth, at the spot where I always knelt, and after that I stopped calling him a glacier and began, without telling anyone, to time my glazing for the hours he was in the room.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Thorvald?
options: She jokes about his slowness while privately seeking out his steady company.
She complains about his pace while waiting for the shelves to be finished.
She respects his care while hoping to make up for the wet pots.
She resents the carpenter comparison while learning to work more squarely.
items.explanation: 화자는 앞부분에서 Thorvald를 '빙하처럼 일한다'며 놀리고, 중간에 '완전히 사실은 아니다'라고 자신의 말을 정정한다. 뒤에서는 그가 자신이 무릎 꿇는 자리의 모서리를 둥글게 다듬은 것을 알아챈 뒤, 남몰래 그가 작업실에 있는 시간에 맞춰 유약 작업을 한다. 따라서 농담 아래에서 그의 곁을 찾는 태도를 말한 A가 정답이다. B는 말투만 읽었고, C는 젖은 도자기에 대한 미안함이라는 다른 이유를, D는 선생님 발언의 어휘를 빌려 정정 어구와 행동을 설명하지 못한다.

items.passage:
Salt crackles under my boots at dawn,
a sound like bread crust breaking,
and I walk the white flat behind the house
the new owner bought with her Vienna money.
Liesel, she says to call her, as if names were cheap.
She asks what to plant where nothing grows;
she asks, again, what she ought to tell her brother
about the father who left this place to strangers.
I tell her salt is honest. I tell her nothing more.
I am not unkind to her, or not exactly.
I say the ground is poor,
the wind is poor, the wages poorer.
But in October I carry pails of river soil
a mile from the road, before she wakes,
and spread them where her window looks,
and set a row of sage there, small and gray,
and when the boy comes visiting at Christmas
I stand back by the shed and let her tell him
that she grew it with her own two hands.
items.question: Which choice best describes the speaker's attitude toward Liesel?
options: He doubts her city habits while expecting her to sell the house soon.
He speaks of her dryly while giving her something to offer her brother.
He helps her in secret while trying to repay a debt to her father.
He prizes honesty while hoping she will tell the boy the whole truth.
items.explanation: 화자 Konrad는 앞부분에서 Liesel의 이름 부탁과 질문을 건조하게 깎아내리고, 중간에 '불친절한 건 아니다, 꼭 그렇지는'이라며 망설이듯 정정한다. 뒤에서는 그녀가 깨기 전에 강 흙을 날라 세이지를 심고, 동생이 왔을 때 그녀가 직접 키웠다고 말하게 둔다. 따라서 무뚝뚝한 말투 아래 그녀가 동생에게 건넬 것을 마련해 주는 태도를 말한 B가 정답이다. A는 말투만 읽었고, C는 아버지에 대한 빚이라는 다른 이유를, D는 'honest'라는 지문 어휘를 빌렸지만 그녀가 세이지를 키웠다고 말하게 두는 행동과 어긋난다.

items.passage: Who returns a gift? Tunde did, the spring he started coming to our seed-saving cooperative in Lima, and I complained about it to anyone who would listen. My father ferries passengers across the river, and I had given Tunde a jar of our best purple corn, saved over four harvests, after he rode with us twice. He brought it back a week later with the lid taped shut and a note listing what he had planted instead. Rude, I called it. A man with manners, I said, would have said thank you and let the jar sit on a shelf. I was not wrong to be annoyed, though perhaps that is not the whole of it. That July I copied his list into the cooperative ledger in my own hand. When the ferry ran late, I kept the front bench free, the one by the window, and did not start the meeting until he came up from the dock.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Tunde?
options: She resents his poor manners while hoping he will apologize for them.
She makes room for him while trying to atone for her harsh words.
She calls his gesture rude while treating his list as worth preserving.
She values the purple corn while doubting the crops he planted instead.
items.explanation: 화자 Valentina는 앞부분에서 선물을 돌려준 Tunde를 무례하다고 여기저기 불평하고, 중간에 '그게 전부는 아닐지도 모른다'며 스스로 말을 누그러뜨린다. 뒤에서는 그의 목록을 협동조합 장부에 손수 옮겨 적고, 그를 위해 앞자리를 비워 둔 채 그가 올 때까지 모임을 시작하지 않는다. 따라서 불평하는 말투 아래 그의 목록을 소중히 여기는 태도를 말한 C가 정답이다. A는 말투만 읽었고, B는 자신의 말에 대한 속죄라는 다른 이유를, D는 지문 어휘를 빌렸지만 장부에 옮겨 적은 행동과 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: Dainius had been retired from the sea for nine years when I moved into the flat beside his, near the old customs checkpoint on the edge of Krakow, and he spent most of my first year, as far as I could tell, telling me what I was doing wrong. My bins stood in the wrong place. My bicycle leaned at the wrong angle. I joked to my sister that he had mistaken the courtyard for a deck and me for a careless deckhand. Then the March storm tore up the strip of earth behind the empty booth, and a rusted tin surfaced there, full of letters in a language neither of us could read. He stood at his window a long while looking at the hole, then drew his curtain. I was not afraid of him, not really; I just preferred the stairs when I heard his door. Still, I was the one who carried the tin to the translator downtown, and I have kept what she told me in my desk drawer, unopened in its envelope, until he asks.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Dainius?
options: She makes fun of his rules while avoiding him whenever she can.
She looks after him while hoping to make amends for her jokes.
She sees him as a stern captain while accepting his rule of the courtyard.
She teases him about his rules while guarding him from unwelcome news.
items.explanation: 화자는 앞부분에서 Dainius가 자신을 갑판원처럼 다룬다며 농담하고, 중간에 '무서운 건 아니다, 정말로는'이라며 망설이듯 정정한다. 뒤에서는 그가 커튼을 친 뒤 화자가 직접 깡통을 번역가에게 가져가고, 그 결과를 그가 물을 때까지 봉투째 보관한다. 따라서 농담 아래에서 그를 원치 않을 수 있는 소식으로부터 지켜 주는 태도를 말한 D가 정답이다. A는 말투만 읽었고, B는 농담에 대한 미안함이라는 다른 이유를, C는 갑판·선장 비유를 빌렸지만 번역을 맡은 행동을 설명하지 못한다.

items.passage: When the ship docked at Accra for supplies, the captain announced that whichever of his two bakers produced the better loaf by evening would keep the galley for the next voyage. Thiago and Ngozi had shared that narrow galley for six years without sharing a single recipe. By late afternoon Thiago's loaf came out black on one side, and he swore that Ngozi had nudged the oven door open as she passed. The cabin boy, who had been peeling yams in the corner, said he had seen Ngozi close the door, not open it. Nobody asked why a sack of Ngozi's own flour lay split on the floor beside Thiago's station. That night the captain tasted Ngozi's loaf and gave her the galley. In the morning, before the ship sailed, she left a second loaf, baked from the flour in the split sack and shaped with Thiago's three-cut top, wrapped in a cloth on the shelf above his bunk. Thiago found it there as he packed and carried it, still wrapped, down the gangway.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: A parting gift recasts an earlier accusation, hinting that the rivalry held unspoken care.
An accusation over a burnt loaf shows how little the two bakers trust each other.
A captain's contest ends with one baker keeping the galley and the other departing.
A baker's guilt over a spoiled loaf leads her to leave a parting gift behind.
items.explanation: 앞부분의 사건은 Thiago가 빵을 태운 책임을 Ngozi에게 돌리는 고발이지만, 목격자는 Ngozi가 오븐 문을 연 것이 아니라 닫았다고 말한다. 뒷부분에서 Ngozi가 Thiago의 방식으로 빵을 구워 남기고 Thiago가 그것을 챙겨 가면서, 앞의 경쟁 장면이 숨은 배려를 담고 있었음이 드러난다. 따라서 두 사건의 관계로 요지를 말한 A가 정답이다. B는 앞 사건만, C는 뒤 사건만 요약하며, D는 Ngozi의 죄책감이 선물의 원인이라고 보아 목격자의 증언과 이어지는 인과를 뒤집는다.

items.passage: Tromso in June never gets dark, and the wedding hall had its curtains open to a sky that refused to end the evening. I had come with an envelope in my jacket: the eight thousand kroner my aunt Wilhelmina had lent me eleven years earlier, when I was nineteen and stranded in Bergen without a ticket home. I found her near the cake table and pressed it into her hand. She looked at the envelope, thanked me for being so generous to the bride, and dropped it into the white box of cards by the door before I could explain. I stood there with my mouth open. Her old wristwatch, I noticed, had stopped at twenty past four, and she did not wind it all night. Hours later, during the speeches, the bride read aloud a card that had been tucked into my envelope, a card I had not written, thanking Devon and Wilhelmina together for their gift. Across the room my aunt raised her glass toward me and turned back to her conversation.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: A nephew's attempt to repay an old loan goes awry at a crowded wedding.
A card read aloud reveals that an apparent mix-up was a way of declining repayment.
A shared card at a wedding shows that the aunt and nephew have grown close.
An aunt's confusion at the wedding leads her to write a card in both names.
items.explanation: 앞부분의 사건에서 Devon은 오래된 빚을 갚으려 하지만 Wilhelmina는 그것을 신부에게 주는 선물로 오해한 듯 상자에 넣는다. 뒷부분에서 그녀가 미리 써 둔 두 사람 이름의 카드가 읽히면서, 앞의 '오해'가 사실은 빚을 돌려받지 않으려는 의도였음이 드러난다. 따라서 두 사건의 관계로 요지를 말한 B가 정답이다. A는 앞 사건만, C는 뒤 사건만 요약하고, D는 혼동이 카드의 원인이라고 보아 미리 준비된 카드라는 단서와 인과를 뒤집는다.

items.passage: Brine and wet stone: that was the smell of the salt-water pool beside the Rhone on the Sunday mornings when Margaux's grandfather took her there. Ahanu swam badly and talked well. Between lengths he taught her words from the language of his childhood, across the ocean: the word for cold water, the word for a river that bends, the word for someone who is late coming home. She repeated them to the tiles and forgot most of them by Tuesday. He would not say who had taught him to swim. In March, fetching his coat from the hook, she found a folded letter addressed to a woman whose name she did not know, written in that language, unsent and creased many times along the same lines. She could read three words of it: cold water, a river that bends, someone late coming home. The following Sunday she arrived at the pool before him, and she was already reciting to the tiles when he came through the door.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: A grandfather's swimming trips become an occasion for teaching his granddaughter words.
A granddaughter discovers an unsent letter her grandfather wrote to an unknown woman.
An unsent letter reveals the weight behind casual lessons, changing how she treats them.
Her eagerness to learn the language leads her grandfather to write an unsent letter.
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 Margaux는 할아버지가 가르쳐 준 단어들을 가볍게 따라 하고 곧 잊어버린다. 뒷부분에서 그 단어들이 할아버지가 부치지 못한 편지 속에 있다는 것을 발견한 뒤, 그녀는 먼저 수영장에 와서 단어를 외우고 있다. 따라서 편지가 수업의 무게를 드러내 그녀의 태도를 바꾼다는 두 사건의 관계를 말한 C가 정답이다. A는 앞 사건만, B는 뒤 사건만 요약하며, D는 여러 번 접힌 오래된 편지를 그녀의 열의가 낳은 결과로 보아 인과를 뒤집는다.

items.passage: I was eleven when I carried the rumor home. Everyone in the school music room said that Siti, who had taught there since before I was born, was being sent away at the end of term, and I repeated it at dinner because it sounded important. My grandfather put down his spoon. He and Siti had not spoken in twenty years, for reasons no one at our table would name, and the next morning he put on his good shirt and walked to the school. I never learned what he said in the headmaster's office. The upright piano in the music room was locked that week, and its key hung on a nail no one would touch. By the cool season the story had come to nothing; Siti was staying. On Saturdays she began coming to our house with a satchel of sheet music, and from the kitchen I could hear two old players arguing over tempo, then starting the same bar again.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: A boy repeats a rumor at dinner and prompts his grandfather to visit the school.
Two old musicians resume playing together at home after many years without speaking.
A grandfather's old quarrel with a teacher causes a rumor about her to spread.
A careless rumor carried home becomes the unexpected route to an old reconciliation.
items.explanation: 앞부분의 사건은 화자가 소문을 집에 옮기자 20년간 말하지 않던 할아버지가 학교로 찾아가는 장면이다. 뒷부분에서 Siti가 토요일마다 집에 와 할아버지와 함께 연주하게 되면서, 앞의 사소한 실수가 두 사람의 화해로 이어졌음이 드러난다. 따라서 두 사건의 관계를 말한 D가 정답이다. A는 앞 사건만, B는 뒤 사건만 요약하고, C는 소문이 화해를 낳은 방향을 오래된 다툼이 소문을 낳았다는 식으로 뒤집는다.

items.passage: Reid came into the laundry house on Thursdays with his violin case under one arm and a bundle of shirts under the other. The steam, he said, kept his strings from going brittle in a Vermont January, and he would tune in the corner while the kettles boiled. I had taught him for six years, and I knew the habit; he tuned twice before every lesson as well. In November the letter had come from the Boston orchestra, a week after the audition date, and I had been the one who left it sealed in my coat pocket. Reid did not mention Boston to me. His first Thursday at the laundry was the week after that date had passed, and on that day he arrived before I did and took the tub beside mine. Each week since, he plays the audition piece once through while my shirts dry on the line. Last Thursday he took down the last of them, folded it collar first, and set it in my basket.
items.question: Based on the passage, why does Reid most likely come to the laundry on Thursdays?
options: To protect his violin strings from the dry winter air while his laundry is washed.
To assure his teacher, without words, that he does not hold the delay against him.
To keep practicing the audition piece in case the orchestra offers him another date.
To remind his teacher, without words, of the audition that the letter cost him.
items.explanation: Reid는 증기가 현을 보호해 준다는 표면 명분을 대고, 앞부분의 조율 습관도 처음에는 그 명분을 지지하는 것처럼 보인다. 그러나 그가 세탁소에 오기 시작한 때가 오디션 날짜가 지난 바로 다음 주이고, 선생님보다 먼저 와 바로 옆 통을 차지했다는 시점 단서가 의미를 바꾼다. 끝에서 선생님의 셔츠를 개어 바구니에 넣는 동작까지 합치면, 편지를 놓친 선생님을 탓하지 않는다는 것을 말없이 보여 주려는 동기인 B가 정답이다. A는 표면 명분, C는 오디션 곡 연습만 설명하며, D는 원망이라는 다른 감정으로 셔츠를 개는 행동과 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: Three rules governed the wall between Kwesi's beekeeper's yard and Kwame's house: no climbing, no smoke on windy days, and no talk of the photograph. Kwame kept the picture in a frame on his side, a print of two boys on one bicycle in front of the old hives, and he hung it in his window every morning facing the yard. Kwesi said he had moved his hives to the far corner years ago because the bees disliked the afternoon heat by the wall. For a long time he worked that corner with his back to the window. In the dry season of 1987, Kwame's son told the street that his father's eyes were failing, and that same week Kwesi began moving the hives, one each evening after dark, toward the wall again. He said nothing to Kwame about it. By March the last hive stood under the window, humming, and each morning Kwesi set a jar of the first honey on top of the wall, its label turned toward the house.
items.question: Based on the passage, why does Kwesi most likely move the hives back toward the wall?
options: To give the bees a better place to forage now that the dry season has arrived.
To reclaim the part of the yard he had given up during their years of distance.
To bring the scene in the picture within reach of a neighbor losing his sight.
To apologize for the years he spent working with his back to the window.
items.explanation: Kwesi는 벌이 벽 근처의 더위를 싫어한다는 표면 명분으로 벌통을 멀리 두었고, 오랫동안 창문을 등지고 일했다. 그런데 Kwame의 눈이 나빠진다는 소식이 퍼진 바로 그 주에, 그는 말없이 밤마다 벌통을 하나씩 벽 쪽으로 옮기기 시작한다는 시점 단서가 동기를 바꾼다. 끝에서 사진 속 벌통 장면처럼 창문 아래 벌통이 웅웅거리고 꿀병의 라벨을 집 쪽으로 돌려 두는 동작을 합치면, 시력을 잃어 가는 이웃이 사진 속 장면을 소리와 맛으로 다시 느끼게 하려는 C가 정답이다. A는 표면 명분, B는 앞의 습관만, D는 미안함이라는 다른 감정으로 소식이 퍼진 시점을 설명하지 못한다.

items.passage: Leopoldina ran the boarding-house kitchen in Porto Alegre by the clock, and she ran me by it too: coffee at five, beans soaking by six, no salt in the pot until she had tasted it herself. When my mother's letter came saying there was work for me with a cousin in Montevideo, my aunt told me I could not possibly go before the feast of Sao Joao, since the house was full and she needed hands. I believed her. The boarders, after all, ate like regiments. But the letter, I saw later, was dated in April, and she gave it to me in June, on the morning after the feast. That week she stopped tasting the pot before I salted it. She let me order from the butcher alone. The night before the ship, she wrapped her own knife, the one with the cracked handle, in a dish towel and laid it at the bottom of my trunk.
items.question: Based on the passage, why does Leopoldina most likely keep the letter from the narrator until June?
options: To keep enough help in the kitchen through the busy feast of Sao Joao.
To keep him from leaving before he could manage a whole kitchen by himself.
To shield him from a cousin's household that she considered unreliable.
To hold on to his company a little longer before letting him go abroad.
items.explanation: Leopoldina는 축제 때문에 일손이 필요하다는 표면 명분을 대고, 앞부분의 엄격한 통제 습관도 처음에는 그 명분을 지지한다. 그러나 편지가 4월에 쓰였는데 축제가 끝난 다음 날 아침에야 건넸고, 그가 혼자 주방을 맡도록 허락한 것은 편지를 건넨 뒤였다는 순서 단서가 동기를 바꾼다. 끝에서 자신의 칼을 그의 짐에 넣어 주는 동작까지 합치면, 그를 떠나보내기 전 조금 더 곁에 두려 한 D가 정답이다. A는 표면 명분이고, B는 독립 훈련이 편지를 준 뒤에야 시작된 순서와 맞지 않으며, C는 사촌에 대한 불신이라는 다른 감정으로 칼을 건네는 행동을 설명하지 못한다.

items.passage: Nandi cut hair on Tuesdays. Her chair was the third from the door in the barbershop on Government Road, and her prices were written in chalk on a slate she wiped every morning. At ten o'clock her sister Eitan came in, after eleven years without a word between them, and sat down in the third chair and asked for a trim. Nandi named the price. Eitan paid it. The scissors went around the left ear, then the right, then the nape, in the order Nandi had learned at fourteen. At the crown she took off half an inch too much, a small bright patch of scalp that no customer would ever see. Eitan did not see it. Nandi set down the scissors and looked at the patch for as long as it took a tram to pass outside. Then she combed the hair over it with her fingers, slowly, the way their mother had combed theirs on Sunday nights, and held up the mirror to the front.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the passage?
options: Clipped and businesslike in manner, tender and regretful toward Eitan
Clipped and businesslike in manner, cool and indifferent toward Eitan
Quiet and restrained in manner, relieved and satisfied toward the unseen error
Quiet and restrained in manner, mournful and grieving toward their mother
items.explanation: 지문 앞부분은 요일, 의자 위치, 가격처럼 건조한 사실을 짧은 문장으로 나열해 사무적인 겉 어조를 만든다. 중간에 Nandi는 아무도 모를 실수 앞에서 전차가 지나갈 동안 멈칫하고, 끝에서는 어머니가 하던 방식으로 머리를 쓸어 덮어 주며 거울을 앞쪽만 비춘다. 따라서 겉은 사무적이지만 속은 언니에 대한 다정함과 회한이 깔린 A가 정답이다. B는 겉 층만 읽었고, C는 실수가 들키지 않은 데 대한 안도로 속 어조의 원인을 뒤집으며, D는 감정의 대상을 어머니로 옮겨 범위를 바꾼다.

items.passage: Thessaloniki was still dark when Despina and I let ourselves into her uncle's bakery to practice, as we had every morning that winter, among the cooling racks. Flour on the music stand. Flour on the bow. Her uncle charged us nothing but the sweeping. The letter from the conservatory in Vienna lay folded inside her violin case, offering one place, for one player, beginning in March. We played the second movement and stopped at the bar where we always stopped. She tuned her A string. I tuned mine. Neither of us said Vienna. Outside, the first cart came for the bread. When we finished, I swept as usual, from the ovens to the door, and then I went back and swept the corner beneath her chair a second time, where there was nothing left to sweep, and set her case by the door with the clasp already fastened.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the passage?
options: Matter-of-fact and orderly on the surface, calm and content toward the routine
Matter-of-fact and orderly on the surface, wistful and resigned toward the parting
Terse and guarded on the surface, bitter and envious toward the scholarship
Terse and guarded on the surface, nostalgic and fond toward the bakery
items.explanation: 지문 앞부분은 '악보대 위의 밀가루' 같은 짧은 조각 문장과 일과의 나열로 담담하고 정돈된 겉 어조를 만든다. 중간에 두 사람은 늘 멈추던 마디에서 멈추고 누구도 빈이라는 말을 하지 않으며, 끝에서 화자는 쓸 것이 없는 자리를 한 번 더 쓸고 상대의 악기 가방을 잠가 문 옆에 둔다. 따라서 겉은 담담하지만 속은 이별을 받아들이는 아쉬움이 깔린 B가 정답이다. A는 겉 층만 읽었고, C는 가방을 챙겨 주는 동작과 맞지 않게 원인을 질투로 뒤집으며, D는 감정의 대상을 빵집으로 옮겨 범위를 바꾼다.

items.passage: "Hold the lamp lower," Kofi said, and Yaa did. She had come to his noodle stall near the Marina with his old school bell in a paper bag, the brass one he had rung for thirty years before the mission school closed, its clapper snapped off at the hinge. She had found a smith in Ebute Metta who would weld it for two shillings. Kofi turned the bell over in his hands between bowls. He tapped the weld with a chopstick. It gave a flat sound, a clack rather than a ring, and a customer at the bench laughed. Kofi laughed too, and ladled the man more broth. He told Yaa the smith had done good work, that the price was fair, and asked after her mother. When she rose to go, he wiped the bell with his apron, front and back, and set it on the shelf above the pot, mouth down, where the steam could reach it every morning.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the passage?
options: Light and good-humored in its telling, cheerful and amused toward the repair
Light and good-humored in its telling, embarrassed and uneasy toward the laughter
Light and good-humored in its telling, tender and wistful toward what cannot return
Gentle and patient in its telling, grateful and proud toward the smith's work
items.explanation: 지문 앞부분은 손님과 함께 웃고 국물을 더 퍼 주는 장면처럼 가볍고 유쾌한 겉 어조로 진행된다. 그러나 중간에 종이 울리지 않고 '딱' 하는 둔한 소리를 내는 디테일이 놓이고, 끝에서 Kofi는 종을 앞치마로 닦아 입을 아래로 향하게 선반에 올려 둔다. 따라서 겉은 유쾌하지만 속은 되돌릴 수 없는 시절에 대한 다정한 아쉬움이 깔린 C가 정답이다. A는 겉 층만 읽었고, B는 웃음에 대한 당혹으로 속 어조의 원인을 바꾸며, D는 감정의 대상을 대장장이의 솜씨로 옮겨 범위를 좁힌다.

items.passage: Four films a week in the season, one in the off-season: that was the rule at the Empire on Frederick Street, and in August even the one played to empty rows. Cecile ran the projector and called the owner Mr. Tomoe, as she had since she was twelve, and he called her Miss Cecile and paid her on Fridays from a tin box. The old doorman who had sold tickets there for forty years lay sick in the back room, asking every evening how the house had been. Tomoe told him full. Cecile said the man deserved to hear the truth. They argued about it on the stairs, politely, and Tomoe had the last word, as owners do. On Friday he opened the tin box and found it heavier than he had left it; the week's takings had been nine shillings, and there were thirty inside. He counted it twice and said nothing. That evening Cecile went into the back room first and told the doorman the house had been full.
items.question: Based on the passage, which choice best describes the relationship between Cecile and Tomoe?
options: Formally his employee, she defers to him as the owner on matters of the theater.
Formally his employee, she challenges his judgment when it comes to the doorman.
Formally his employee, she relies on his generosity to keep her place at the theater.
Formally his employee, she covers his losses in secret and yields to his wishes.
items.explanation: 앞부분의 'Mr. Tomoe', 'Miss Cecile'라는 호칭과 금요일 급여는 공식적인 고용 관계를 보여 준다. 그러나 중간에 주간 수입보다 훨씬 많은 돈이 깡통에 들어 있어, 실제로 비용을 조용히 대는 쪽이 Cecile임이 드러난다. 끝에서 그녀는 진실을 말해야 한다던 주장을 접고 먼저 들어가 도어맨에게 '만석이었다'고 말한다. 따라서 겉으로는 고용인이지만 그의 손실을 몰래 메우고 그의 뜻에 양보하는 관계를 말한 D가 정답이다. A는 호칭만, B는 계단 장면만 반영했고, C는 깡통 단서와 반대로 의존 방향을 뒤집는다.

items.passage: "Sit if you're staying, Master Ronan," Fergus said, and went on chalking the coat on his table. He had called me that since my father sailed for Boston, as if I were a customer and not a boy who had sat in his back room every evening for three months waiting for the post. I sat on the bolt of grey serge. He did not offer tea; he never did. At six the post boy came with nothing for us, and Fergus marked it in the ledger by the door, in the column he kept for my father's letters, a column of short dashes. When my boots split in October, a new pair appeared under the serge with no bill attached. I asked him what I owed. He said the account was settled and named no one who had settled it. On the last night before the news came, I fell asleep on the bolt and woke to find the lamp still lit and Fergus sitting up at the table with no coat in front of him.
items.question: Based on the passage, which choice best describes the relationship between Fergus and Ronan?
options: Though he speaks to Ronan formally, Fergus has taken up the duties of a guardian.
Though he speaks to Ronan formally, Fergus keeps a tradesman's distance from him.
Though he speaks to Ronan formally, Fergus relies on him for company in the evenings.
Though he speaks to Ronan formally, Fergus shares his worry each time the post arrives.
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 Fergus는 Ronan을 손님처럼 'Master Ronan'이라 부르고 차도 내주지 않아 거리를 두는 듯 보인다. 그러나 중간에 아버지의 편지를 장부에 기록하고, 계산서 없이 새 부츠를 마련해 준 뒤 누가 값을 치렀는지 말하지 않아 비용을 조용히 떠맡는 쪽이 Fergus임이 드러난다. 끝에서 그는 일감도 없이 밤새 등불을 켜 둔 채 소년 곁을 지킨다. 따라서 보호자의 역할을 맡은 관계를 말한 A가 정답이다. B는 호칭만, D는 우편 장면만 반영했고, C는 돌봄의 방향을 뒤집는다.

items.passage: Two herrings on Mondays, a smoked eel on Thursdays, and no credit: those were the terms Herr Gyeongho set when Katharina first came to his stall at the edge of the omnibus depot in Hamburg. She called him Herr Gyeongho, and he called her Fraulein, and they bargained each week over a pfennig as if the stall depended on it. In the winter her mother's wages from the depot laundry stopped. Katharina still came on Mondays and Thursdays and paid what she could, and he wrapped the fish without counting the coins. One afternoon, sent to fetch paper from under his counter, she opened the wrong drawer and found a ledger in her own family's name, page after page of small debts, every line crossed through in the same blue pencil. She closed the drawer. The next Monday she brought him a pfennig more than the price and set it on the scale before he could speak; he looked at it a long moment and let it lie there.
items.question: Based on the passage, which choice best describes the relationship between Katharina and Gyeongho?
options: Behind their formal bargaining lies a plain trade between a merchant and a regular buyer.
Behind their formal bargaining lies a protective generosity he extends to her family unseen.
Behind their formal bargaining lies a shared pleasure in haggling that both look forward to.
Behind their formal bargaining lies his reliance on her custom to keep the stall afloat.
items.explanation: 앞부분의 'Herr', 'Fraulein'이라는 호칭과 외상 불가 규칙, 매주의 흥정은 공식적인 상거래 관계를 보여 준다. 그러나 중간에 그는 돈을 세지 않고 생선을 싸 주고, 서랍 속 장부에는 그녀 가족의 빚이 모두 같은 연필로 지워져 있어 비용을 조용히 떠안은 쪽이 그임이 드러난다. 끝에서 그는 그녀가 더 얹은 동전을 말없이 받아 들여 그녀의 체면을 지켜 준다. 따라서 그가 그녀 가족을 보이지 않게 돕는 관계를 말한 B가 정답이다. A는 호칭과 규칙만, C는 흥정 장면만 반영했고, D는 의존의 방향을 뒤집는다.

items.passage: Hokkaido in February looked, from the overnight train, like a page no one had written on yet. I had no ticket. I had climbed into the last compartment at Sapporo because its blind was down, and the old man inside, whose cap still said CAPTAIN in faded thread, moved his feet to make room and went on looking out the window. For three hours neither of us spoke. At each station he took a brass compass from his coat, opened it, checked our heading against the timetable on his knee, and snapped it shut. When the conductor's steps came down the corridor, he set the compass on the seat between us, open, and kept his eyes on the glass; the conductor glanced at the cap and moved on. Near Asahikawa he spoke at last, to ask where I was going. I told him I did not know. He held out the compass, still open, closed my fingers around it, and lay back with his cap over his eyes.
items.question: In the passage, the compass most likely represents
options: a navigational tool he uses to confirm the train's progress at each stop.
the order and routine of his former life at sea, which he still keeps up.
a sense of purpose he hands on to someone who has not yet found one.
the trust between the two travelers, which his long silence had withheld.
items.explanation: 처음에 나침반은 노인이 역마다 열차의 방향을 확인하는 도구로 등장한다. 중간에 차장이 다가오자 그는 나침반을 열어 두 사람 사이 좌석에 놓아 화자를 감싸는 데 쓰고, 끝에서는 갈 곳을 모른다는 화자의 손에 열린 나침반을 쥐여 주는 동작으로 바뀐다. 따라서 두 맥락을 모두 포괄해, 방향을 잃은 사람에게 넘겨주는 삶의 방향 감각을 뜻하는 C가 정답이다. A는 문자적 기능, B는 앞 맥락만 반영했고, D는 침묵을 관계의 단절로 보아 나침반을 건네는 마지막 동작의 의미를 관계 회복으로 잘못 읽는다.

items.passage: By the time I came back to Oaxaca, nine years after I had left without a note, Ksenia's shoe repair stall had moved two streets closer to the market, but the shelf behind her bench was the same. On it, among the heels and polish tins, sat my old school shoes, the black ones with the buckle she had replaced three times the year I was ten. She used them, I saw that first morning, as a stand for her spare awls, the points tucked into the toes. She did not ask where I had been. I did not offer. For a week I swept her floor and handed her tacks while she talked to customers about soles. On the eighth day, while I was sweeping, she took the shoes down, shook the awls out into a tin, and rubbed both shoes with black polish until the scuffs went dark. Then she set them on the bench beside my broom, laces loosened, next to her own work boots.
items.question: In the passage, the old school shoes most likely represent
options: a pair of shoes Ksenia once mended for a child who was growing fast.
a part of the past that Ksenia had put to practical use and set aside.
a wound Ksenia had carried through the absence, which the polishing closes.
a place held through the years that she now offers back without demands.
items.explanation: 처음에 학교 구두는 Ksenia가 송곳을 꽂아 두는 실용적인 받침으로 선반에 놓여 있다. 그러나 화자가 돌아와 일주일을 함께 보낸 뒤, Ksenia는 송곳을 털어 내고 구두를 닦아 화자의 빗자루 옆, 자신의 작업화 곁에 끈을 풀어 놓아 둔다. 그녀가 어디 있었는지 묻지 않았다는 점까지 합치면, 구두는 그동안 지켜 온 자리를 조건 없이 다시 내주는 것을 뜻하므로 D가 정답이다. A는 문자적 의미, B는 앞 맥락만 반영했고, C는 송곳이 꽂힌 구두를 상처로 보아 관계의 손상·회복으로 잘못 읽는다.
